claim: The prefrontal cortex (PFC)'s functions are thought to include working memory, as its activity can reflect information that must be temporarily maintained to realize the current goal.
source: The prefrontal cortex (PFC)'s functions are thought to include working memory, as its activity can reflect information that must be temporarily maintained to realize the current goal.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature establishing PFC's role in working memory.

claim: Across a broad population of PFC neurons, there was no evidence of current-goal-specific memory in any previously reported form (differences in the rate, sequence, phase, or covariance of firing).
source: However, across a broad population of PFC neurons, we found no evidence of current-goal-specific memory in any previously reported form – that is differences in the rate, sequence, phase, or covariance of firing.
evidence: This is the primary finding of the study, supported by multiple analyses presented in the manuscript including firing rate analysis, sequential pattern analysis, phase analysis, and covariance analysis.

claim: The PFC grouped locations representing behaviorally equivalent task features together, consistent with a role in encoding long-term knowledge of task structure.
source: Instead, the PFC grouped locations representing behaviorally equivalent task features together, consistent with a role in encoding long-term knowledge of task structure.
evidence: This claim is supported by the t-SNE analysis shown in Figure 6D and related analyses.

claim: The prefrontal cortex plays a central role in flexible goal-directed behavior.
source: The prefrontal cortex (PFC) plays a central role in flexible goal-directed behavior (Miller and Cohen, 2001; Fuster, 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: One of the PFC's primary functions is thought to be the maintenance of information relevant for achieving the current goal (i.e. working memory).
source: and one of its primary functions is thought to be the maintenance of information relevant for achieving the current goal (i.e. working memory) (Fuster and Alexander, 1971; Funahashi et al., 1989; Miller et al., 1996; Rainer et al., 1998; Romo et al., 1999; Wang, 1999; Erlich et al., 2011; Wimmer et al., 2014; Inagaki et al., 2019; Wu et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Rodent spatial working memory experiments employed to date with recording in PFC or other brain areas have not combined all elements of flexibility (distractions, different start locations, different unpredictable routes, and more than two goals) in a single task.
source: However, rodent spatial working memory experiments employed to date with recording in PFC or other brain areas (Wood et al., 2000; Frank et al., 2000; Baeg et al., 2003; Fujisawa et al., 2008; Gill et al., 2011; Harvey et al., 2012; Pfeiffer and Foster, 2013; Wikenheiser and Redish, 2015; Ito et al., 2015; Spellman et al., 2015; Kim et al., 2016; Guise and Shapiro, 2017; Bolkan et al., 2017) have not combined all of these elements of flexibility in a single task.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature and serves as justification for the current study design.

claim: Rats reached high levels of performance in the multi-start/multi-goal/multi-route task (mean performance: 77.37%, 95% CI: [72.46, 81.97]).
source: Animals reached high levels of performance (Figure 1C,D, mean performance over all rats: 77.37, 95% confidence interval [CI]: [72.46, 81.97]).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data presented in Figure 1C,D.

claim: The performance was comparable across routes for all animals, indicating that rats remembered goal locations instead of routes.
source: The performance was comparable across routes for all animals, indicating that rats remembered goal locations instead of routes (Figure 1D, left).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral analysis comparing performance across different routes, shown in Figure 1D.

claim: In trials where the goal was adjacent to the available route, rats most often took the shortest route (88%, 81%, and 95% of trials for each animal, respectively).
source: In trials where the goal was adjacent to (i.e. 60 degrees in either direction from) the available route, rats most often took the shortest route (88%, 81%, and 95% of trials for each animal, respectively), supporting the idea that animals used a spatial map instead of a fixed route plus recognition strategy.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data analysis.

claim: The performance was comparable and above chance for all goal locations, implying that rats remembered each goal location rather than relying on a strategy of remembering only a subset of them.
source: Furthermore, the performance was comparable and above chance for all goal locations, implying that rats remembered each goal location rather than relying on a strategy of remembering only a subset of them (Figure 1D, center left).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: A Neuropixels probe was chronically implanted in medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC).
source: A Neuropixels probe (Jun et al., 2017a) was chronically implanted in medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), previously shown to be required in variants of simpler rodent spatial working memory tasks (Spellman et al., 2015; Guise and Shapiro, 2017).
evidence: This is a methodological statement supported by the experimental procedures described.

claim: One hundred to two hundred units were simultaneously recorded across subareas including anterior cingulate, prelimbic (PL), infralimbic, and dorsal peduncular cortices.
source: One hundred to two hundred units were simultaneously recorded across subareas including anterior cingulate, prelimbic (PL), infralimbic, and dorsal peduncular cortices (Figure 1B) (n = 3 animals: 182, 131, and 98 cells in the three main sessions analyzed, one from each animal; in addition, for two animals, one novel rotation experiment session each, consisting of 152 and 186 cells, was used for the analysis of relearning).
evidence: This is a methodological statement describing the recording data.

claim: The population vector at each goal during the sample phase was distinguishable and stable over time.
source: To begin with, the PV at each goal during the sample phase was distinguishable and stable over time (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), including across sample and test phases (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the correlation analysis and decoding results shown in Figure 2A and supplementary figures.

claim: The overall activity during the delay period was not more correlated with the currently remembered goal's population vector than with other goals.
source: Having established the presence of a stable spatial representation at each goal, we correlated the overall activity during the delay period with the sample phase PV at each goal and asked whether it was more correlated with the currently remembered goal's PV. This was not the case (Figure 2B)
evidence: This claim is supported by the correlation analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The remembered goal was not decodable from delay period activity using correlation-based classification with a wide range of time bins.
source: While the animal's current (i.e. start) location was readily decodable (as expected), the remembered goal was not, using a wide range of time bins (Figure 2C)
evidence: This claim is supported by the decoding analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: No single-cell activity in 100-ms- to full-delay-period-sized time bins showed consistent firing differences for allocentric, start-dependent, or egocentric goal location.
source: We initially tested if any single-cell activity in 100-ms- to full-delay-period-sized time bins showed consistent firing differences for allocentric, start-dependent, or egocentric goal location (Figure 3—figure supplement 2). We found significant differences for the current (i.e. start) location, but not allocentric or egocentric goal location.
evidence: This claim is supported by the H-score analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Current location could readily be decoded with any classification method for time bin resolutions between 100 ms to the full delay period duration.
source: Results were consistent across methods and time resolutions: current location could readily be decoded with any classification method for time bin resolutions between 100 ms to the full delay period duration.
evidence: This claim is supported by the classification results shown in Figure 3C.

claim: No classification method could successfully classify the remembered goal in allocentric or egocentric coordinates at any time resolution.
source: In contrast, no method could successfully classify the remembered goal in allocentric or egocentric coordinates at any time resolution (Figure 3C), including when using all cells regardless of firing rate stability (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by the classification results shown in Figure 3C and supplementary figures.

claim: Performance dropped dramatically after the maze was rotated by 60 degrees, then gradually improved over the remainder of the session.
source: Consistent with the idea that the animals must adapt to the new configuration and learn to apply previously internalized rules, performance dropped dramatically then gradually improved over the remainder of the session (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from the rotation experiment shown in Figure 4A.

claim: During relearning after maze rotation, population analysis still could not decode the currently remembered goal during the delay period.
source: However, during this relearning, when the cognitive demand might be higher and thus elicit a more prominent representation of critical task variables, population analysis still could not decode the currently remembered goal during the delay period.
evidence: This claim is supported by the decoding analysis during relearning shown in Figure 4B,C.

claim: Spatial representation of the start locations was clearly represented even as the animal adapted to the new configuration after maze rotation.
source: In contrast, spatial representation of the start locations was again clearly represented even as the animal adapted to the new configuration (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the decoding analysis during relearning shown in Figure 4B,C.

claim: The distributions of phase preference magnitudes for different goals were not different from shuffled data, suggesting the remembered goal does not affect overall phase preference.
source: We compared the distribution of phase preference magnitudes to one where goal labels were shuffled. The distributions were not different, neither when including all stable cells, nor when selecting only cells that showed significant overall phase locking, suggesting the remembered goal does not affect overall phase preference (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the phase analysis shown in Figure 5A and supplementary figures.

claim: Spike counts at specific phases did not differ in a goal-specific manner.
source: Second, we asked whether spike counts at specific phases might differ in a goal-specific manner, either when using all stable cells or only those that were significantly phase locked to at least one of the goals, but they did not (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the phase-based decoding analysis shown in Figure 5A and supplementary figures.

claim: Neither for pairs of neurons exhibiting excitatory interactions nor for pairs exhibiting inhibitory interactions did covariances differ between trials associated with one goal versus the others.
source: However, neither for the pairs of neurons exhibiting excitatory interactions nor for the pairs of neurons exhibiting inhibitory interactions did covariances differ between trials associated with one goal versus the others (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 2, see Materials and methods).
evidence: This claim is supported by the covariance analysis shown in Figure 5B and supplementary figures.

claim: Previously described forms of working memory maintenance are not responsible for storing the current goal in this task requiring flexible information use.
source: Together, these results suggest that previously described forms of working memory maintenance are not responsible for storing the current goal in our task in which this information must be employed flexibly.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the multiple negative findings from different analyses.

claim: It was possible to decode the currently remembered goal location from the neural data at various time points outside the delay period.
source: Importantly, we performed these analyses not only using the neural data but also, separately, using the position tracking data of the two LEDs on the animal's head. We found that it was possible to decode the currently remembered goal location from the neural data at various time points.
evidence: This claim is supported by the time-resolved decoding analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: The remembered goal could also be decoded from the behavioral tracking data alone with a very similar time course to neural decoding.
source: However, the remembered goal could also be decoded from the behavioral tracking data alone with a very similar time course.
evidence: This claim is supported by the comparison of neural and behavioral decoding shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: The neural representation of the currently remembered goal at various time points outside the delay period is likely due to the animal's position, orientation, posture, or other behavioral features.
source: Thus, it is likely that this neural representation of the currently remembered goal at these times is due to the animal's position, orientation, posture, or other behavioral features (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is an inference based on the similarity between neural and behavioral decoding time courses.

claim: The decoding performance based on tracking data was at chance levels throughout the nose poke delay period.
source: Crucially, the decoding performance based on tracking data was at chance levels throughout the nose poke delay period (Figure 3—figure supplement 4, third row, right, period from −3 to 0 s), providing direct evidence that our task design reduces the presence of confounding behavioral variables during that period.
evidence: This claim is supported by the behavioral decoding analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: Activity at the goal in the sample phase did not differ when there was an error in the subsequent test phase versus when there was not.
source: First, we analyzed if the activity at the goal in the sample phase (presumably during encoding) differs when there is an error in the subsequent test phase or not, but this was not the case.
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: After the animal had made an incorrect choice in the test phase, activity at the goal was markedly different, presumably due to the lack of reward.
source: In contrast, after the animal had made an incorrect choice in the test phase, activity at the goal was markedly different, presumably due to the lack of reward; however, correlations between the PVs of activity at the goal among correct trials and, separately, among error trials was comparable (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: mPFC delay period activity did not indicate an upcoming or past error.
source: Furthermore, mPFC delay period activity did not indicate an upcoming or past error (Figure 6B), further corroborating that mPFC might not directly store current memory content.
evidence: This claim is supported by the decoding analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Task phase was not decodable before reaching the center and at the center when animals returned from the goal.
source: Before reaching the center, and at the center, task phase was not decodable (Figure 6C) (note the decodability afterwards could arise from cue or behavior differences in the two phases that were not present earlier).
evidence: This claim is supported by the decoding analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Within each group of behaviors (waiting at a start nose port, crossing a bridge/route, consuming reward at a goal), mPFC displayed spatial selectivity.
source: Lastly, we compared the population activity while rats engaged in different behaviors at different locations. Within each group of behaviors (i.e. waiting at a start nose port, crossing a bridge/route, consuming reward at a goal), mPFC displayed spatial selectivity (e.g. it differentiated the three bridges).
evidence: This claim is supported by the t-SNE analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: This spatial selectivity was embedded within a larger organization of activity in which distinct, task-relevant groups were clearly separable from each other.
source: Furthermore, we found that this spatial selectivity was embedded within a larger organization of activity in which these distinct, task-relevant groups were clearly separable from each other (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the t-SNE analysis shown in Figure 6D and supplementary figures.

claim: Previous work has shown sensory stimulus-specific delay period activity independent of motor plans or resistant to distractor stimuli in the PFC.
source: Previous work has shown sensory stimulus-specific delay period activity (delay activity) independent of motor plans (Romo et al., 1999; Wu et al., 2020) or resistant to distractor stimuli (Miller et al., 1996)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Previous work has shown start-independent spatial or route-independent visuospatial goal-specific delay activity in the PFC.
source: and start-independent spatial (Brown et al., 2016; Guise and Shapiro, 2017; Watrous et al., 2018) or route-independent visuospatial (Saito et al., 2005) goal-specific delay activity in the PFC.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: A pair of studies using a single start location showed no evidence of goal-selective delay activity in rodent PL mPFC.
source: A pair of studies (using a single start location; Spellman et al., 2015; Bolkan et al., 2017) showed no evidence of goal-selective delay activity in rodent PL mPFC.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Spatial information is strongly represented in PFC in primates and essentially all rodent studies, including the current study.
source: Spatial information is strongly represented in PFC in primates (Funahashi et al., 1989; Rainer et al., 1998; Saito et al., 2005; Lara and Wallis, 2014) and essentially all rodent studies, including here (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Figure 3—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature and data from the current study.

claim: The current study found no spatial goal-selective delay activity despite spatial information being strongly represented in PFC.
source: Spatial information is strongly represented in PFC in primates (Funahashi et al., 1989; Rainer et al., 1998; Saito et al., 2005; Lara and Wallis, 2014) and essentially all rodent studies, including here (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Figure 3—figure supplement 1); yet, we found no spatial goal-selective delay activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by the negative findings from the current study contrasted with the presence of spatial representations.

claim: The ability to decode the current start position and also the goal at various time points during the task, and the relatively high number of cells recorded simultaneously, suggests that the data set was large enough to have detected an effect of sizes previously reported in the literature for simpler tasks.
source: Furthermore, our ability to decode the current start position and also the goal at various time points during the task (Figure 3—figure supplement 4), and the relatively high number of cells recorded simultaneously in our study, suggests that our data set was large enough to have detected an effect of sizes previously reported in the literature for simpler tasks.
evidence: This is an inference based on the successful decoding of other variables and the sample size.

claim: In contrast to previous studies, the current study combined all elements of flexibility in one task – distractions, different start locations, and different unpredictable routes, as well as more than two goals.
source: In contrast to previous studies, we combined all elements of flexibility in one task – distractions, different start locations, and different unpredictable routes, as well as more than two goals.
evidence: This is a methodological statement describing the unique features of the task design.

claim: The study found no evidence of goal-selective delay activity in fully trained animals or during relearning in any of the major forms previously documented over a wide range of parameters and across large numbers of simultaneously recorded cells in multiple mPFC subareas.
source: We found no evidence of goal-selective delay activity in fully trained animals or during relearning in any of the major forms previously documented over a wide range of parameters and across large numbers of simultaneously recorded cells in multiple mPFC subareas.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main findings.

claim: Canonical representations of working memory (as previously described) are unlikely to serve as general working memory correlates that can be employed under conditions of high behavioral flexibility.
source: Thus, these representations are unlikely to serve as general working memory correlates that can be employed under conditions of high behavioral flexibility, such as those often encountered in the real world.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the negative findings of the study.

claim: The strikingly similar time course of goal decoding using either neural or behavioral tracking data outside of the well-controlled delay period demonstrates potential confounds resulting from task-related variables.
source: For instance, the potential confounds resulting from such task-related variables are seen in the strikingly similar time course of goal decoding using either neural or behavioral tracking data outside of the well-controlled delay period (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of neural and behavioral decoding.

claim: The results suggest a role for mPFC in working memory tasks by representing task structure in terms of groups of behaviorally related elements.
source: Finally, our results suggest a role for mPFC in working memory tasks by representing task structure in terms of groups of behaviorally related elements (Jung et al., 1998; Yu et al., 2018; Kaefer et al., 2020), consistent with findings that the PFC forms long-term memories of learned stimulus categories (Freedman et al., 2001).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings supported by citations to related literature.

claim: All procedures were conducted in accordance with the Janelia Research Campus Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee.
source: All procedures were conducted in accordance with the Janelia Research Campus Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee.
evidence: This is a statement about ethical compliance.

claim: The chronic Neuropixels implant surgery followed previously described methods.
source: The chronic Neuropixels implant surgery followed previously described methods (Jun et al., 2017a).
evidence: This is a methodological statement supported by citation.

claim: Rats learned the MSMGMR task over the course of several months in successive learning steps with generally one learning session per day.
source: Rats learned the 'multi-start/multi-goal/multi-route' (MSMGMR) task over the course of several months in successive learning steps with generally one learning session per day.
evidence: This is a methodological statement describing the training procedure.

claim: Data from three male Long-Evans rats were included in this study.
source: Data from three male Long-Evans rats were included in this study.
evidence: This is a methodological statement describing the subjects.

claim: Between training sessions, the maze was wiped with 70% ethanol to reduce any odor cues animals might use to navigate to the correct goal.
source: Between training sessions, the maze was wiped with 70% ethanol to reduce any odor cues animals might use to navigate to the correct goal.
evidence: This is a methodological statement describing experimental controls.

claim: The maze was mounted on a turntable-like frame and rotated to one of three orientations in between sessions, to further lower the probability that animals used local cues to remember goal locations.
source: Furthermore, the maze was mounted on a turntable-like frame and rotated to one of three orientations in between sessions, to further lower the probability that animals used local cues to remember goal locations.
evidence: This is a methodological statement describing experimental controls.

claim: The initial drop in performance observed after the rotation of the maze in the relearning experiments is in line with animals using distal, non-local cues for navigation.
source: The initial drop in performance we observed after the rotation of the maze in the relearning experiments (Figure 4) is in line with animals using distal, non-local cues for navigation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the behavioral results from the rotation experiment.

claim: Neural data from Neuropixels '1.0' probes was recorded with SpikeGLX software.
source: Neural data from Neuropixels '1.0' probes (https://www.neuropixels.org) was recorded with SpikeGLX software (http://billkarsh.github.io/SpikeGLX/).
evidence: This is a methodological statement describing data acquisition.

claim: Three hundred and eighty four channels were recorded simultaneously across subareas of the mPFC in two separate frequency bands (spike: 300 Hz to 10 kHz sampled at 30 kHz and LFP: 0.5–300 Hz sampled at 2.5 kHz).
source: Three hundred and eighty four channels were recorded simultaneously across subareas of the mPFC in two separate frequency bands (spike: 300 Hz to 10 kHz sampled at 30 kHz and LFP: 0.5–300 Hz sampled at 2.5 kHz).
evidence: This is a methodological statement describing data acquisition parameters.
